storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — radar is clear, there are no weather alerts, and the air is dry and stable, so the cove gets the same quiet, cooling evening as the towns around it.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The cool layer over the 65°F Sound is already too thin to matter (5°F air–water gap at 4 PM, 4°F by 5 PM, gone by 6 PM as the air cools) — and there are no storms around for it to act on.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: quiet. The KOKX radar scan at 3:51 PM shows no storm cells anywhere in the approach sector, there are no active NWS alerts, and the model shows zero storm energy (CAPE 0 J/kg). Pressure is steady near 1019–1020 hPa and the air is dry (dew points in the low-to-mid 40s) under a west-northwest flow — a fair-weather pattern.

Wind aloft is strong but has nothing to work with. The change in wind between the surface and about 20,000 ft is large (about 67 kt from the west), which on an unstable day would organize storms. With no instability and no moisture, it is irrelevant tonight.

Local effects: neither of the cove's usual modifiers is in play. The Sound is 65°F and the air about 70°F, so the air–water gap is only 5°F at 4 PM — already at the edge of the ~5°F needed for a meaningful stable layer over the water. The Sound holds its temperature while the air cools toward sunset (6:22 PM), so that gap shrinks to about 4°F by 5 PM and disappears by 6 PM. There is no sea breeze either: only 1 of 19 coastal stations has any southerly wind. With no storms inbound, none of this changes the outcome — the cove sees the same weather as inland towns.

Most likely outcome: dry and clear through the evening, turning partly cloudy overnight with a low near 47°F.

What would change the call: nothing visible for tonight. The National Weather Service discussion mentions a wetter system later in the forecast period (heavy rain and an isolated thunderstorm possible, mainly NYC and west, depending on its track) — that is beyond this evening and will be picked up in later updates.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind fading to light after sunset — no sea breeze in play

hourly.shift_note: dropping fast toward sunset (6:22), puffs and holes

wind.tactics_blurb: Gusty west-northwest wind off the land is at its best right at 5 PM and fades quickly — about 5 kt by sunset and a near-drifter after 8 PM. Stay center-course to keep your options open, tack on the headers, and sail to the puffs coming off the northwest shore; get the racing in early.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of day: a moderate gradient-wind day with no sea breeze in play. The wind is the large-scale west-northwest flow, not a thermal: the air–water temperature difference is only 4.9°F (a sea breeze needs at least 5°F and this one is shrinking), and just 1 of 19 coastal stations shows any southerly wind. Well-sited airport and waterfront anemometers average 10 kt, and stations across the region agree on WNW (81% within 45° of the 289° median).

Now at Riverside YC: NW 309° at 15 kt gusting 19, with a 10-minute average of 11 kt. The mid-Sound buoy reads the same NW 309° at 13 gusting 20 (that reading is about 75 minutes old).

Through the window: this wind will not hold its strength. Both the HRRR model and the National Weather Service hourly forecast take it from about 9 kt at 5 PM to 4–6 kt by 6 PM, then 3–5 kt through the evening. That is not a sea breeze dying — it is a land breeze under clear, dry skies: as the ground cools around sunset (6:22 PM) the air near the surface goes still and stops mixing down the stronger wind above it. Offshore flow like this is the direction most prone to that evening shut-off. Expect direction to creep from WNW toward NW as it lightens.

Where the pressure is: wind from this quarter comes over land, so it arrives in puffs with holes between them and swings of 15–25° either side of the average. The best average pressure is usually mid-cove, away from the lee of the trees and houses on the northwest shore; the puffs fan out from that shore. No side pays consistently, which is why the call is center — play each shift rather than banking on a corner. As the breeze drops below about 6 kt, connecting puffs matters more than the shifts.

What racers will feel: at 5 PM, 8–10 kt with gusts in the mid-teens — good dinghy racing, briefly powered up in the puffs. By 6 PM it is a 4–6 kt light-air race, and from 8 PM on it is 3–4 kt, marginal for racing at all. A first race is comfortable; later starts are at risk of becoming drifters.

Model versus stations: the HRRR model has the wind at WNW 289°, western-Sound stations at 297°, and Riverside YC itself at NW 309°. The table shifts the model about 8° right to match the stations. Because this is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day, the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply. No sign of a cold push from the northeast either: Boston, Providence and Groton are all still west to west-northwest.

data_caveats: HRRR model data only reached 6 PM this run (forecast hours beyond f03 were not yet available) — the 7–10 PM wind rows are based on the National Weather Service hourly forecast and the model's fading trend, so treat them as lower confidence.
